clue.text: Believe dog to be delicate creature

parts.note: to swallow a story is to believe it
to dog or tail someone is to follow them closely

explanation.surface: Someone credits their pet dog with being a fragile little thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Believe' and 'dog' look like a statement about a pet, but both are verbs: swallow (accept credulously) and tail (follow).
explanation.definitionFit: The swallowtail is a butterfly, and a butterfly is a classic example of a fragile, delicate insect.

clue.text: Old dreamer's single winter blanket?

parts.note: surface: an old man dreaming under a single winter bedcover; setter's reading: the old hit song (a 'single') about dreaming, sung by Bing Crosby
surface: a bedcover for cold nights; setter's reading: a blanket of snow lying over the festive day

explanation.surface: An elderly sleeper makes do with just one blanket in winter.
explanation.walkthrough: The dreamer is the singer of 'I'm dreaming of a ...', the famous 1942 record, and the blanket is snow; 'single' is the record, not the bed.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's title names a festive day with snow on the ground, a snowy blanket in winter, and it was a hit single.

clue.text: Large pond, bit of snow skimmed off?

indicators.note: skimming takes off the very top layer, so the first letter of the word is removed

parts.note: a snowflake is a small piece of snow

explanation.surface: Someone skims a snowflake off the surface of a big pond.
explanation.definitionFit: A lake is a body of standing water, jokingly a pond on a large scale.

clue.text: Absurd disagreement beginning in Yorkshire, increasingly interminable in English county

indicators.note: the letters so far are placed inside the county's name

parts.note: Oxon is the standard abbreviation for Oxfordshire

indicators.note: without a termination, so the word loses its final letter
the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that letter is used

explanation.surface: A county quarrel that began in Yorkshire grows without end.
explanation.walkthrough: Oxon is the short form of Oxfordshire, from its Latin name.
explanation.definitionFit: An oxymoron joins contradictory terms, like 'deafening silence', so it is a self-disagreement that sounds absurd.

clue.text: Father with prize lifted up, big daddy!

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifting the letters up means reading them from the bottom, so they run backwards

parts.note: a pot is a trophy, a prize cup

explanation.surface: A dad hoists a trophy above his head in triumph.
explanation.definitionFit: Big daddy is slang for the dominant person, the boss, which is what the phrase for the leader of the pack means.

clue.text: Regularly find clue is not doing a lot

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the words is taken

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: A solver who keeps finding the clue sits there doing little.
explanation.definitionFit: Being inactive or lazy is exactly doing very little; the adjective fits after 'is'.

clue.text: Royal advisor in red, certainly blue backfiring

parts.note: cardinal is a deep scarlet colour

indicators.note: something backfiring goes the wrong way, so these two words are read in reverse

explanation.surface: A royal counsellor dressed in red finds a blue plan going wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The red is apt: Thomas Wolsey, Henry VIII's chief minister, was a cardinal and wore cardinal red.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Wolsey was the chief minister and counsellor to King Henry VIII.

clue.text: Drunk resisted new drink

indicators.note: a drunk person's words come out jumbled, so these letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A drunk turned down yet another drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' is tempting as the abbreviation N, but here all three letters are needed in the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: A dessert wine is a sweet wine served with pudding, a kind of drink.

clue.text: Critical accident in cinema upset crime writer

indicators.note: the first two words go inside the scrambled cinema
upset means knocked over and disordered, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: a spill is a small accident or tumble

explanation.surface: A serious mishap at the pictures upsets an author of thrillers.
explanation.definitionFit: Mickey Spillane was the American author of the hard-boiled Mike Hammer detective novels.

clue.text: Fine, give up attempt on goal

parts.note: to kick a habit is to give it up

explanation.surface: Pay a fine, then give up on goal-scoring.
explanation.definitionFit: In football a penalty kick is a free shot at goal from the penalty spot.

clue.text: Old PM back in the office

indicators.note: the back of a word is its end, so only its last letter is taken

parts.note: a den is a private room used as a study or office

explanation.surface: A former Prime Minister returns to work at his desk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back in the office' reads as one phrase, but it splits: the back of 'the', then the office. Anthony Eden was UK Prime Minister in the 1950s.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Anthony Eden was British Prime Minister from 1955 to 1957, so he is a former premier.

clue.text: Element reverend originally introduced to blessing

indicators.note: the single letter is put inside the following word

parts.note: a boon is a blessing or benefit

indicators.note: originally points to the origin of the word, its opening letter

explanation.surface: A vicar first brings a blessing into a ceremony.
explanation.definitionFit: Boron is a chemical element, number 5 in the periodic table.

clue.text: Novel does for poetry

definitions.note: a mass noun standing for a plural: odes are pieces of poetry

indicators.note: novel means new, so the word is made anew in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A novel will do as well as poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like the book; it is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Odes are lyric poems, so collectively they are poetry.

clue.text: Property equally prepared

explanation.surface: A house shared fifty-fifty, all ready to go.
explanation.definitionFit: An asset is something owned that has value, a piece of property in the financial sense.

clue.text: Cart full of insects?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a light vehicle or pushchair
second meaning, a playful one: infested with bugs

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the jokey second sense: the adjective formed from bug.
explanation.definitionFit: A buggy is a small cart or carriage, and anything crawling with bugs could be called buggy.

clue.text: Bond: he is back, a gentleman outwardly?

indicators.note: back means turned round, so the little word goes the other way
outwardly says the next words sit on the outside, surrounding the rest

parts.note: a Spanish gentleman, as in Don Quixote

explanation.surface: James Bond is back, a gentleman spy, at least on the outside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bond' suggests 007, but it is the plain word for sticking together. Only 'is' turns round; 'he' stays as it is.
explanation.definitionFit: Adhesion is the sticking together of surfaces, a bond between them.

clue.text: Groove — or tap?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a groove or rail along which something slides
second meaning, a whimsical one: a tap is something that runs

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers the jokey sense: water runs from a tap, so a tap is a thing that runs.
explanation.definitionFit: A slide or track a drawer moves along is called a runner, and anything that runs, like a tap, can whimsically be one.

clue.text: Game tied, foul in baseball area

indicators.note: game here means up for anything, willing to be rearranged into another order

explanation.surface: A tied game is decided by a foul during a baseball match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' reads as the match; it is the adjective meaning willing, the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The outfield is the grassy part of a baseball diamond beyond the infield where outfielders stand.

clue.text: Joint finally loosened up worked

indicators.note: finally points to the very end of the word, its last letter

explanation.surface: A stiff joint was at last eased with oil, and the machine worked.
explanation.definitionFit: To toil is to work hard; the past tense matches 'worked'.

clue.text: Sense of cake's lightness, might one say, around a home?

parts.note: a bun is a small cake

indicators.note: around says the preceding letters wrap about the single letter that follows

parts.note: a glow is a gentle light

explanation.surface: A baker muses on how light a sponge is, around the house.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'might one say' admits the whimsy: a cake's light would be its 'bun glow', which then wraps round A.
explanation.definitionFit: A bungalow is a single-storey house, a type of home.

clue.text: Treble, say — scorcher?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a treble is an example of a vocalist, the boy soprano
second meaning, a whimsical one: something that singes

explanation.walkthrough: 'say' marks the treble as one example of the class; the question mark flags the jokey second reading built from singe.
explanation.definitionFit: A treble is a type of vocalist, and a thing that scorches or singes could fancifully be called this.

clue.text: Stuff body of sea bird

indicators.note: the body of a word is its middle, between head and tail, so only the central letter is kept

explanation.surface: Stuff the carcass of a seabird, like a taxidermist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'body of sea' looks like an expanse of ocean; it means the middle letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The kite is a bird of prey of the hawk family, such as the red kite.

clue.text: Second jack questionable

parts.note: J is the abbreviation for jack in cards

explanation.surface: A second jack in the pack looks suspicious.
explanation.definitionFit: A jiffy is an informal term for a very short moment, just like 'a second'.

clue.text: Fleece wrapped around right ear

indicators.note: one word is wrapped about the other, so it surrounds it

parts.note: to fleece someone is to con them
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A woolly fleece is wrapped round someone's right ear to keep it warm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ear' is not the organ but the seed head of a cereal plant.
explanation.definitionFit: An ear is the grain-bearing head of a cereal, which is corn.

clue.text: Scrap material covering shoe, once

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a short cloth gaiter worn over the shoe and ankle, now old-fashioned

explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrap' looks like a bit of material; it is a squabble.
explanation.definitionFit: A spat is a minor row, and spats were old cloth coverings buttoned over the upper of a shoe.

clue.text: Coalition basically liberal or conservative, first of all

indicators.note: the first of all the words means taking the opening letter of each one

explanation.surface: A political alliance that is at heart either liberal or conservative.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloc is a group of parties or nations allied for a common purpose, a coalition.

clue.text: Victor sang, Gaels played flute

indicators.note: the words are played around with, rearranged like notes in a tune

explanation.surface: Victor sang while some Scots and Irish played the flute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flute' sounds musical alongside 'sang' and 'played', but it is the tall narrow glass.
explanation.definitionFit: A flute is a tall, narrow stemmed glass used for sparkling wine.

clue.text: Experimenting with a cold pet, try old reptile

indicators.note: experimenting means trying things out in different ways, so the letters are tried in a new order

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

explanation.surface: A scientist experimenting with a cold-blooded pet tries out an old reptile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old reptile' reads as the definition, but 'old' belongs to the mix; the definition is just 'reptile'.
explanation.definitionFit: The pterodactyl was a prehistoric flying reptile of the dinosaur age.
